nameStory: This aquatic plant gets its colorful name from its bright green, feathery leaves that emerge above the water surface like the plumes on a parrot's head. The delicate, finely-divided foliage resembles the soft, layered feathers of tropical birds, creating an eye-catching display that makes this invasive species unfortunately easy to love.
description: Parrot's feather is an aquatic plant that grows partially submerged in ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams. It produces bright green, feathery stems that emerge 4-12 inches above the water surface, creating dense mats of soft, delicate foliage. The plant spreads aggressively through underground stems called rhizomes, forming thick carpets that can cover large areas of water. Though pretty to look at, it's actually an invasive species from South America that can clog waterways.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Feathery, bright green leaves arranged in whorls of 4-6 around the stem, feeling soft and delicate like fine hair when touched underwater

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Stems emerge 4-12 inches above water surface while roots anchor in muddy bottom, forming dense floating mats

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny, inconspicuous white or yellowish flowers appear where leaves meet the stem on emerged portions

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Submerged portions feel slippery and soft, while emerged stems are firmer but still tender enough to break easily

idTips.label: Arrangement
idTips.description: Leaves divided into thread-like segments that collapse when removed from water, unlike stiff terrestrial plants

habitat: Found in ponds, lakes, slow streams, and quiet backwaters throughout New England's lower elevations. Prefers shallow areas with muddy or sandy bottoms where it can root, typically in water 1-10 feet deep. Often grows alongside cattails, water lilies, and native pondweeds in disturbed aquatic habitats.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as water warms, with bright green shoots pushing up through the water surface. This is when the plant is most actively spreading through underground runners.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with lush, bright green foliage creating dense surface mats. Small flowers may appear on emerged stems during hot weather.
seasonality.fall: Foliage begins to yellow and die back as temperatures drop, though some green growth may persist into early winter in protected areas.
seasonality.winter: Most above-water growth dies back, but roots and lower stems survive under ice, ready to resprout when water warms again.

funFact: Parrot's feather is so aggressive that in many New England states it's illegal to sell, transport, or plant this species - yet it continues spreading because tiny plant fragments can travel on boat propellers, fishing gear, or even waterfowl feet to start new colonies miles away!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with native water milfoils, but parrot's feather is the only milfoil with bright green stems that stick up noticeably above the water surface. Native milfoils typically stay submerged or barely reach the surface, and their foliage is usually duller green or reddish.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its beauty, parrot's feather is considered one of New England's most problematic aquatic invasives. It was originally sold as an aquarium and water garden plant, but escaped cultivation and now threatens native aquatic ecosystems by forming dense monocultures that crowd out native species.
compareHints: Unlike its native milfoil cousins that stay mostly submerged, parrot's feather boldly emerges above water with bright green foliage. Eurasian water-milfoil (also invasive) tends to have reddish stem tips and stays closer to the surface, while native milfoils like whorled water-milfoil have much more subdued coloring and growth habits.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Eurasian water-milfoil has more finely divided leaves than most of its native relatives, with leaflets that are thread-like and numerous.
Among New England's water-milfoils, broadleaf water-milfoil stands out for having distinctly broader surface leaves compared to most relatives like Eurasian water-milfoil.
Low water-milfoil is the shortest member of its genus in New England, staying under a foot tall while Eurasian water-milfoil can reach 10 feet long.
Among New England's water-milfoils, Slender Water-milfoil lives up to its name with the most delicate, thread-like leaf divisions.
Unlike the aggressive Eurasian water-milfoil which forms dense mats, alternate water-milfoil grows in looser colonies and has its distinctive alternately-arranged flowers rather than whorled ones.
Siberian water-milfoil differs from other milfoils by its relatively short flower spikes and less aggressive spreading habit compared to invasive species like Eurasian water-milfoil.
Unlike the invasive Eurasian water-milfoil which has leaves scattered along the stem, whorled water-milfoil has its distinctive whorled leaf arrangement.
